findings.title: Denial cache key omits identity type, poisoning across principals
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey builds a key from namespace, userUID, action, name and parent only, with no identity type. Anonymous subject 'anonymous:0' and render subject 'render:0' both resolve to UID '0', so they share the identical denial key for the same namespace/action/resource. Service.Check checks this denial cache first and returns Allowed:false on hit without evaluating permissions. Consequence: a denial cached for anonymous causes a later renderer check for the same dashboard/folder to be denied without ever consulting renderer wildcard logic, and any user/service-account UID overlap across types shares the same fate, causing false denies for up to the 30s TTL.

findings.title: Denial cache short-circuits fresh DB read, preserving stale denies
findings.body: Check looks up permDenialCache and on hit immediately returns Allowed:false without consulting cached permissions or the database. Denial entries are set after a DB-backed deny and live 30 seconds with no invalidation. If access is granted after the denial was cached, for example a newly created dashboard/folder grant or role change, checks for that same name+folder within the TTL still deny even though the DB would now allow. This defeats the PR's own fallback that requeries the DB when cached scopes miss, because the denial hit prevents that fallback. Consequence: newly granted access remains invisible until expiry.

findings.title: Every cached deny triggers DB fetch, nullifying permission cache
findings.body: After a denial-cache miss, Check loads cached permissions; if they hit but checkPermission returns false it falls through to getIdentityPermissions which queries the DB for identifiers, roles, teams and permissions. Previously a cached scope map served denies without DB work. Now every Check for a distinct resource the user lacks access to costs full DB queries, with the per-resource denial cache only helping repeats of the exact same name+parent. Enumerating many random names or normal deny-heavy traffic causes one DB permission fetch per distinct resource. Consequence: large latency and DB load regression and easy DoS amplification.

findings.title: List serves stale cached permissions with no outdated-cache fallback
findings.body: List calls getCachedIdentityPermissions and if it hits uses that scope map directly to build the response, only querying the DB on cache miss. Unlike Check there is no revalidation when the cached map is outdated. If the per-user/action permCache entry was populated before a dashboard/folder was created or granted, List omits the new item until the 30s entry expires. Consequence: the stated goal of letting users fetch newly created dashboards/folders still fails on the List path.

findings.title: Folder hierarchy cache not refreshed on deny, breaking inherited grants
findings.body: checkInheritedPermissions calls buildFolderTree which returns the cached folderTree if present and otherwise never refreshes it on permission denial. Check's new fallback refreshes permission scopes from the DB but leaves the folder tree stale. If a child folder or dashboard is created under a parent the user can access, the stale tree lacks the new node so Ancestors/Children lookups still fail, the check denies even with fresh scopes and then caches a per-resource denial. Consequence: new nested folders/dashboards relying on inherited folder permissions stay inaccessible until the folder cache expires.

findings.title: DB fallback reuses stale team and role caches, missing new team grants
findings.body: getUserPermissions, used for the fallback DB read, first calls getUserBasicRole and getUserTeams which return cached values when present. The subsequent permissionStore.GetUserPermissions query is built from those possibly stale team IDs and role. If access was newly granted via team membership or basic-role change, the fallback still queries with old teams/role and returns no permission, so Check denies and caches denial. Consequence: requerying permissions from the DB does not fix freshness for team/role-driven grants until those caches expire.

findings.title: Denial key concatenation ambiguous, distinct resources share entry
findings.body: The denial key is namespace + '.perm_' + userUID + '_' + action + '_' + name + '_' + parent with plain underscore separators and no escaping. Different tuples collide, for example name 'a_b' with parent 'c' produces the same suffix as name 'a' with parent 'b_c', and UIDs or actions containing underscores add more collisions. Since dashboard/folder UIDs can contain underscores, two distinct resources can map to the same denial key. Consequence: a denial cached for one resource falsely denies an unrelated resource for up to the TTL.
